doc.title: Mike Longo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2019

title: The thread through jazz and Dizzy's new swing
summary: A blues thread links Hawkins and Coltrane; Dizzy's music was an evolution, and bebop found a new way to swing.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Of course. There’s a thread that runs through all of jazz, the real stuff. That’s why if you listen to that record with Coltrane and Coleman Hawkins, they’re playing together. Two totally different styles, but there’s a thread that holds them together. I would say the thread has more to do with the blues. And so all those guys, I’ve always been able to play the blues from when I first started. And so that’s the thread. Now somebody like Coltrane, he’s playing all that intervallic stuff he was playing, he’s playing with Coleman Hawkins and they’re playing together. The music is going together. And so I played a long time, before I went with Dizzy I was playing with Roy Eldridge here in town. And Roy is the one that went and got Dizzy and told him, “Come here, you’ve got to hear this piano player you know.” But Roy, that thread was there you know. And the swing. The swing is the — now as jazz has evolved through the stages what evolved was a new way to swing.

Yeah. Dizzy’s music, say Count Basie swung but that ain’t the same swing that Dizzy played with. If you think about Freddie Green going ching-ching-ching, you can’t do that to a tune [scats]. See how do you do that? And so what Dizzy and them did was found a new way to swing. A new kind of beat and all that. But that’s how jazz has evolved over the time. And so Dizzy took issue with a guy in England that was interviewing him that was talking about the bebop revolution. He said it wasn’t a revolution it was an evolution. Because Dizzy, Charlie Parker, he could play with a hillbilly band and sound good.
